about.title: Livermore Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely feels like a legal matter in the moment. You're on the ground in a Livermore grocery aisle, a downtown parking structure, or a neighbor's back patio, and the first thought is simply whether you can stand up. Only later does the real question arrive: should someone have caught that hazard before you did? Under California premises liability law, that question is the heart of the case. An owner or occupier is generally responsible when they knew, or reasonably should have known, about a spill, loose stair tread, or unlit path and failed to repair it or warn people. Proving that notice takes evidence, and in Livermore evidence disappears quickly. Store cameras overwrite footage within days, spills get mopped, and a cracked curb outside a business along Isabel Avenue gets patched before anyone photographs it. LawProactive is a free connection service, not a law firm. We match people injured across Alameda County with an independent attorney who takes premises cases on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Livermore Fall Victims Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Notice is the whole fight
items.desc: California asks whether the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys in our network know how to pull inspection logs, maintenance records, and prior complaints that show how long a problem sat unaddressed.

items.title: Video and photos vanish fast
items.desc: Most commercial cameras in Livermore keep footage for a short window before it is overwritten. Getting a preservation demand out early, along with your own photos of the scene, can be the difference between a documented hazard and a disputed memory.

items.title: Deadlines and shared blame are manageable
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, but the window is far shorter when a public entity owns the property. California's pure comparative fault rule also means being partly at fault reduces a claim rather than ending it.

items.question: I fell at a Livermore city park or public building. Is the process different?
items.answer: Yes, in an important way. When the property belongs to a public entity such as the City of Livermore or Alameda County, California requires a formal government claim on a much shorter timeline than the usual two-year deadline. Missing that early step can close the door on the case entirely. An attorney can sort out who actually owns or controls the property and get the claim filed correctly.

items.question: I was looking at my phone when I slipped. Do I still have a case?
items.answer: Possibly. California follows pure comparative fault, so a jury or insurer can assign you a percentage of responsibility, and your recovery is reduced by that share rather than eliminated. The owner's failure to clean up, repair, or warn still counts. An attorney can evaluate how those percentages might realistically shake out before you decide anything.

items.question: What should I do in the first few days after a fall in Livermore?
items.answer: Get medical attention first, even if the pain seems minor, because fall injuries often worsen over a day or two. Photograph the hazard, your footwear, and the surrounding area, and write down names of any witnesses or employees who saw it. Ask the business in writing to preserve its surveillance footage, since many systems record over themselves within a week. Then reach out, and we'll connect you with an independent attorney who can take it from there.
